What is sustainable construction?

Sustainable construction aims to reduce the environmental footprint and hence the use of natural resources such as energy, water and materials to the maximum extent. This is achieved by using materials that are renewable or contain recyclable content avoiding the adverse impact of extracting and processing virgin materials, minimizing energy consumption and waste going to landfill.

How does Oberoi Realty lower its impact on the environment?

At Oberoi Realty, we create living spaces with a lower impact on the environment by following stringent, international, product guidelines. 

We aim to source 20-40% of the energy consumption of our owned, commercial buildings from renewable energy sources. 

We measure and manage the energy, water and waste footprints of our owned assets.

How does Oberoi Realty maintain biodiversity at its projects?

Our projects are developed in accordance with green building norms such as the preservation of topsoil, use of native plant species and preserving or replanting a minimum number of trees on our sites. We design our buildings to reduce the Urban Island Heat Effect and maintain the microclimate of the site through our landscape design.

How do you reduce water consumption at projects?

Water is an important but scarce resource for our industry. Our water conservation efforts during construction include monitoring our water use from various sources to reduce potable and non-potable water. We design holistic water management programs for the occupancy phase of our developments including the use of low flow fixtures, STPs for recycling 100% of domestic water and reuse of up to 40% of STP water for landscaping and flushing.

Does Oberoi Realty use renewable sources of energy?

Alternate and sustainable energy sources are paramount in transitioning to a net zero economy. Keeping this in mind, several of our commercial developments source a significant proportion of their energy demand from renewable sources such as solar and wind. We aim to provide onsite renewable energy to the maximum extent possible in our residential developments.

How do you manage waste?

We measure all waste associated with our construction processes such as demolition, excavation and construction. We make provisions for holistic waste management and suitable disposal from our construction sites. 

All our projects segregate waste into dry and wet and further process wet waste through OWCs on site. The dry waste from our developments is removed by vendors for further processing.

# The business of ecosystems: How Oberoi Realty justifies its 15% market premium 

## Sarina Menezes, Senior VP of Marketing at Oberoi Realty, details how the company uses a "pull" marketing strategy for its ultra-luxury estates to build trust with HNI homebuyers. 

Kausar Madhyia 

 06 Apr 2026 05:30 IST

Sarina Menezes, Senior VP of Marketing and Corporate Communications at Oberoi Realty

For those who still read newspapers, it will not come as a surprise to find that every high-rise-glass-clad building in India now comes with a luxury, or better yet, ultra-luxury tag attached to it. 

While for some real estate giants it may mean swimming pools or pickleball courts, for Sarina Menezes, senior VP of marketing and corporate communications at Oberoi Realty, luxury means a quiet simplicity in exchange for the “biggest cheque you will write in your life”.

> View this post on Instagram

Oberoi Realty is a real estate developer that prides itself on curating integrated human-centric developments in the form of high-end residential, commercial, and hospitality ecosystems. It operates in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, Thane and Gurugram. 

According to a Money Control report, Oberoi Realty made a revenue of Rs 4,558 crore in FY2025, up almost threefold from its Rs 1,629 crore revenue in FY2023.

## Betting on experience centres

The word ‘ecosystems’ is generously used by the developer, as it believes in creating integrated infrastructure where its biggest priority is to enable its residents “to walk to work”. 

> "Luxury is an experience," Menezes says. "It's something that has to be tangible and has to meet with the intangibles that you actually walk into." To ensure this goal, the brand pioneered "experience centres" rather than mere sales galleries. 

According to Menezes, one can easily determine the luxury quotient of goods and services with immediate possession. However, since one has to wait for at least four years to experience their luxury home, "we want our customers to actually experience the brand right when they interact with us for the first time" through experience centres.

## Distraction-free marketing for distraction-free living

Oberoi’s marketing strategy is as minimalist as its designs. In a move that defies industry norms, the brand utilises a "pull" strategy, shying away from festive events or "pushy" sales tactics. Unlike other luxury developers, Oberoi Realty prefers to invite its guests to its experience centres rather than host them at Diwali- or Christmas-themed events. 

Even the company's visual language is strictly product-focused.

"The events and the activities are a distraction from the product," Menezes explains. "Any luxury product cannot have distractions around it. Even in the creative works or films we use, you will never see a human being in them. It’s very clean, very timeless, and very product-focused because people can be a distraction to the product."

## 'New urbanism' and 'biophilia'

Menezes says that Oberoi has adopted the philosophy of "new urbanism", which focuses on building not just homes but entire communities where residents can not only walk to work or school but also to luxury five-star hotels.

Whether it’s the 80-acre "amoeba-shaped" development built around a natural hillock or the Forestville project inspired by "biophilia", the goal is human-centric design, she adds. 

> Menezes describes biophilia as a design that is "influenced by nature, air, light, and water. Every home will have light coming in and the right amount of wind". 

Since creating such communities requires a massive land parcel, usually, the Oberoi estates are located on the outskirts of the city with limited dining options. Hence, the developer also has high-end restaurants such as Bodega, Chin Chin and KOKO built directly into its developments to ensure the residents do not have to drive for a good meal. 

> View this post on Instagram

## Catching the "pickleball" wave

Oberoi is moving beyond building homes to curating a lifestyle that justifies its 15% premium. As Menezes puts it, while others promise luxury and deliver "reality", Oberoi stands for designs that remain timeless, even 18 years later.

For Oberoi, staying at the top of the pyramid means listening to a demographic of 30-to 40-year-olds who have travelled the world and demand global standards. Menezes reveals that they often leave amenity details for the final stages of a five-year project to ensure they remain relevant.

"If I had not planned for pickleball six years ago, you would not get a pickleball. You have to keep your ear to the ground and make sure your ecosystem is relevant to today’s next-gen buyers. I cannot build for my earlier buyers."

This adaptability has led to unique additions like a bowling alley in Three Sixty West Mumbai at Worli and a rooftop "sky garden" experience in Borivali featuring toughened glass floors.

## The trust factor and the power of print

With price points starting at Rs 7 crore in some micro-markets and reaching Rs 150,000 per square foot at Three Sixty West Mumbai in Worli, Menezes acknowledges that credibility is their strongest currency. "This is the biggest cheque you will write in your life, and you will definitely give it to someone you trust."

Surprisingly, for a brand chasing the next-gen, Oberoi remains a staunch believer in print media. Why print still? “It’s the first thing an Ultra-HNI would pick up in the morning with his breakfast. It’s about presenting your brand to the customer when he wakes up first thing in the morning."

At Oberoi Realty, they don't just sell square footage; they sell the luxury of forgetting you’re in Mumbai entirely.
